## Source-level findings and prospective learning objectives

The following are independently summarized evidence notes for subsequent question authorship, not MCQs, mock slots, historical exam evidence or a claim of comprehensive uniqueness.

### Routine adult triage
Source: [WHO IITT FAQ](https://cdn.who.int/media/docs/default-source/integrated-health-services-%28ihs%29/csy/iitt/iitt-faq.pdf), questions 3, 6–9 and 13–16. PDF extracted text inspected, screenshot failed. [Official tool overview](https://www.who.int/tools/triage) HTML opened.
- T1: Prioritize clinical sorting before administrative intake or payment.
- T2: Ensure acuity assessment even when a bed is readily available, since treatment may still be delayed.
- T3: Record the assigned category as part of communication and quality oversight.
- T4: Escalate highest-acuity patients to immediate resuscitation care.
- T5: Reassess waiting patients under facility protocols when deterioration is possible.
- T6: Distinguish acuity assignment from diagnosis and disposition decisions.
- T7: Use locally defined time goals rather than claiming universal yellow/green waiting intervals. Red requires immediate attention.
- T8: Use trained clinical staff, not untrained security personnel, for routine clinical triage.

### Resuscitation quality
Source: [AHA 2025 Adult BLS](https://cpr.heart.org/en/resuscitation-science/cpr-and-ecc-guidelines/adult-basic-life-support), sections 7.2 and 7.3, HTML recommendations and supportive text inspected.
- B1: Minimize interruptions surrounding defibrillation and restart compressions promptly after shock.
- B2: Limit professional pulse checks during rhythm assessment to ten seconds, resume compressions if pulse is uncertain.
- B3: Coordinate compressor rotation around two minutes when additional rescuers are available.
- B4: Interpret compression fraction as actual compressing time divided by total resuscitation time. The guideline describes at least 60% as a reasonable minimum target with qualified recommendation strength, not a universal guarantee of outcome.
- B5: Assess feedback-device trends for depth, rate and recoil rather than assuming one acceptable metric establishes good CPR.
- B6: Address rescuer ergonomics and the support surface without avoidable treatment interruption.

### Transfer and trauma safety
Sources: [WHO Acute Transfer Checklist](https://cdn.who.int/media/docs/default-source/integrated-health-services-%28ihs%29/csy/ect/acute-transfer-checklist.pdf), steps 1–3; [WHO SBAR](https://cdn.who.int/media/docs/default-source/integrated-health-services-%28ihs%29/csy/bec-slides/bec/sbar.pdf); [NICE QS174 structured handovers](https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/qs174/chapter/Quality-statement-4-Structured-patient-handovers); [WHO Trauma Care Checklist](https://cdn.who.int/media/docs/default-source/emergencies-trauma-care/trauma-congress-630_a3e8707b-6cd6-4482-a3cf-70019f677abe.pdf?download=true&sfvrsn=3a553ced_8). PDF text extracted, screenshots failed. Trauma checklist second-page encoding defective, do not infer unreadable details. NICE HTML opened.
- H1: Compare risk of transport with unavailable care benefit and provide appropriate stabilization before transfer without needless delay.
- H2: Confirm receiving service acceptance and required clinical support during transport.
- H3: Convey response to interventions, clinical trajectory, next action, urgency and contingency plan during structured handover.
- H4: Obtain receiver confirmation of essential information to address misunderstandings.
- H5: Send relevant records with the patient and verify arrival and condition afterward.
- H6: Use trauma checklist at the end of primary/secondary assessment and before the team leaves the bedside.
- H7: Transfer explicit ongoing monitoring plans and unfinished care tasks in addition to diagnostic labels.

### Facility mass-casualty response
Sources: [WHO facility MCM triage guidance](https://cdn.who.int/media/docs/default-source/integrated-health-services-%28ihs%29/csy/mcm-triage_guidance-note.pdf), pages 3–4; [WHO MC-IITT FAQ](https://cdn.who.int/media/docs/default-source/integrated-health-services-%28ihs%29/csy/mc-iitt-faq.pdf); [WHO mass casualty management toolkit](https://www.who.int/teams/integrated-health-services/clinical-services-and-systems/emergency-and-critical-care/mass-casualty-management). PDF text inspected, screenshots failed, official HTML toolkit opened.
- D1: Use surge triage when the facility's incident plan is activated, rather than equating every multiple-patient arrival with mass casualty conditions.
- D2: Apply the surge triage process to all arrivals, including unrelated medical emergencies.
- D3: Preserve one-way patient movement and avoid bottlenecks in emergency resuscitation spaces.
- D4: Reassess ambulatory patients for deterioration rather than treating initial walking status as permanent low acuity.
- D5: Locate delayed-care monitoring near escalation resources but apart from immediate resuscitation capacity.
- D6: Distinguish senior-clinician blue-category decisions under present resource constraints from abandonment. Continue appropriate supportive/palliative care and reassess as capacity changes.
- D7: Assign registration and labeling support separately from clinical prioritization where staffing permits.
- D8: Keep track of location and clinical status through patient tracking and accompanying records.
